cta_body: This is the one audit in the Day-1 set that ends with advice not to pitch yet. SunSource's website is fully offline and its operating portfolio was sold in January 2026. If you want, Smart Pursuit will re-qualify the entity and tell you in 48 hours whether there is a business here to sell to. Reply or WhatsApp 7095024220.
ad_intro: This audit reached a different conclusion from every other lead in the Day-1 set, and the recommendation is to pause outreach rather than send it. On 14 Sep 2026 sunsourceenergy.com is completely offline - not slow, not misconfigured, but returning no response at all on https or http. Independently, in January 2026 SunSource sold roughly 300 MWp of its operational solar portfolio to Inox Neo Energies, and headcount is reported at 97, down 38% year on year. A funnel audit of a site that does not load is not the useful deliverable here. What follows is what the evidence actually supports: a status assessment, and the conditions under which this becomes a lead again.
ad_intelligence: Fully offline. https://sunsourceenergy.com and the www host both fail at the SSL handshake (SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL, no response); plain http returns an empty reply from server. Independent fetch attempts return HTTP 500. This is not a rendering bug - there is no site to audit.

~45 active Meta ads with a WhatsApp destination at an estimated sub-Rs.1 lakh/month. Given the site is down, the ad count must be re-verified in Meta Ad Library India before it is treated as real - the Day-1 figure may be stale, and any creative pointing at the website is pointing at nothing.

Wholly owned subsidiary of SHV Energy (Netherlands), which took a majority stake in May 2021 and committed roughly Rs.1,800 crore to grow capacity from 65 MW to 550 MW. Neev Fund (SBI + UK Government) exited at that point.

5 January 2026: Inox Clean Energy's IPP arm Inox Neo Energies acquired ~250 MWp of operational solar projects from SunSource, with a further ~50 MWp pending approvals - ~300 MWp total, across 13 states, held via multiple SPVs, on PPAs averaging ~24 years.

The acquired portfolio supplies Britannia Industries, Jubilant Foodworks, Hitachi Energy and Max Healthcare, among others - the marquee C&I logos SunSource built its reputation on now sit with the acquirer.
findings: 1. The website is not slow or broken - it is gone. Every access route tested on 14 Sep 2026 failed: https://sunsourceenergy.com and https://www.sunsourceenergy.com both die at the SSL handshake with SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL and no response; http://sunsourceenergy.com returns 'Empty reply from server'; independent page-fetch attempts return HTTP 500. There is no holding page, no redirect to an SHV Energy property, and no maintenance notice. For a company whose buyers are CFOs and facility heads signing 24-year power purchase agreements, a corporate domain that does not resolve is the most damaging possible signal - it reads as insolvency whether or not that is the case.

2. The operating portfolio - the thing being advertised - was sold in January 2026. On 5 Jan 2026 Inox Clean Energy announced that Inox Neo Energies had acquired ~250 MWp of SunSource's operational solar projects, with another ~50 MWp in process, totalling ~300 MWp across 13 states including Uttar Pradesh, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra. Those assets carried long-term PPAs averaging ~24 years with Britannia, Jubilant Foodworks, Hitachi Energy and Max Healthcare. In C&I solar the installed portfolio is the sales pitch - it is the reference list, the credit proof and the case-study library in one. Any campaign still running on those logos is marketing assets that now belong to Inox.

3. The organisation has contracted sharply. Headcount is reported at 97 as of mid-2025, a 38% year-on-year decline, and the company is classified as acquired. Co-founder Kushagra Nandan has left to build LNK Energy, announced in January 2026 with a stated Rs.10,000 crore five-year plan across solar manufacturing, green fuels and renewable power - after an earlier venture, REnergy Dynamics, in 2024. A shrinking team, a departed co-founder and a divested portfolio are three independent signals pointing the same direction.

4. The Day-1 leak is now unanswerable rather than merely unfixed. The stub flags 'no case-study PDF or site-survey scheduler for facility heads'. That was a fair criticism of a functioning C&I business. Today there is no site on which to host a case study, and the projects that would have populated those case studies belong to another company. The correct response is not to build the asset - it is to establish first whether SunSource is still selling new C&I capacity in India at all, or whether SHV Energy has repositioned it.

5. Roughly 45 creatives are reportedly live against infrastructure that cannot receive them. If the Day-1 count is accurate, every click is landing on a dead domain. The WhatsApp destination may still be answered - which is the one thing worth testing - but with no site, no pixel, no landing page and no form, there is zero attribution, zero retargeting and zero measurable intent. Even at under Rs.1 lakh a month, that is pure waste, and worse, it is actively broadcasting the dead domain to the market. Recommendation: verify the ad count in Meta Ad Library India and, if live, pause everything until the site is restored.

6. What genuinely remains, if the entity is still trading. The history is real and it is good: founded 2010 by Adarsh Das and Kushagra Nandan; one of India's first rooftop solar public-private-partnership projects; a 21 MWp plant at Ramanathapuram, Tamil Nadu commissioned Aug 2024 with SuperGas as an anchor offtaker; a stated 500 MWp portfolio under contract and development at that time; presence across data centres, metals and mining, automotive, chemicals, cement, healthcare and pharmaceuticals; and the backing of SHV Energy, a 125-year-old Dutch multinational. If SunSource is still writing new PPAs under SHV, that parent covenant is the strongest asset it has - a C&I buyer signing for 24 years is buying the balance sheet behind the panels, not the panels.

7. The honest recommendation: do not send a performance-marketing pitch to this lead yet. Every other audit in this set ends with a 48-hour, 7-day and 14-day plan. This one should not, because the prerequisite is unresolved. Pitching CPL optimisation to a company that may be winding down its India C&I operation wastes the prospect's time and damages the sender's credibility. The correct next action is a qualification call, not a sales call - and if the answer is that SHV is recapitalising SunSource for a new build-out, then this becomes a genuinely attractive account with a parent balance sheet behind it and a website that has to be rebuilt from scratch anyway.
wins: Step 1 - qualify the entity before spending an hour on creative

Three checks, all doable in a day. Confirm in Meta Ad Library India whether the ~45 creatives are genuinely live and where they point. Message the WhatsApp number from the ads and see whether a human replies and what they say they sell. Check SHV Energy's own corporate communications for SunSource's current status in India. Until those three come back, this is not a prospect - it is an open question.
Step 2 - if the entity is trading, the first deliverable is the website itself

There is no funnel work to do because there is no funnel. Restoring sunsourceenergy.com, or formally redirecting it to an SHV property, is prerequisite zero - a C&I buyer evaluating a 24-year PPA will Google the counterparty, and right now that search ends in a connection error. Only after the domain resolves is there any point discussing case-study PDFs, a site-survey scheduler or ABM.
Step 3 - if there is a new build-out, the pitch writes itself

A restored SunSource under SHV Energy has an unusually strong C&I story: a 125-year-old Dutch multinational parent, 15 years of Indian distributed-solar history, the Ramanathapuram 21 MWp plant, and the credibility of having built a portfolio substantial enough for Inox to buy. Lead with the parent covenant, publish the surviving projects as dated case studies, add a site-survey scheduler for facility heads, and run LinkedIn ABM against CFOs and plant heads rather than broad Meta. That is a real engagement - but only after Steps 1 and 2.
